observations.quote: the Generation, Dignity, & Excelency OF THE MICROCOSM, Or Little World MAN
observations.what: the Generation, Dignity, & Excelency OF THE MICROCOSM, Or Little World MAN
observations.note: The heading announces the subject of the section: the Generation, Dignity and Excelency of man, named the Microcosm or Little World.

observations.quote: THE MICROCOSM, Or Little World MAN
observations.note: The heading sets three names side by side for one thing: Microcosm, Little World, Man.

observations.quote: For a man to know God & lightly esteem of his own selfe is the highest and profitable knowledge
observations.note: The margin note at the head of the paragraph calls knowing God and esteeming oneself lightly the highest knowledge.

observations.quote: the most excellent Phylosophy is that which enlightens the mind to the right knowledge of it selfe
observations.note: The best philosophy is defined by its object: the mind's right knowledge of itself.

observations.quote: to be ignorant of that knowledge is the greatest shame and most pestilent disease of the mind
observations.note: Not knowing oneself is called a shame and a disease of the mind.

observations.name: Trismegistus
observations.quote: Ignorance, saith Trismegistus to his Son Tat, is the greatest Enemy and principall Tormenter in every Man
observations.note: A saying on ignorance given to Trismegistus, spoken to his son Tat, in support of the point on ignorance.

observations.name: Luke 16.
observations.quote: who neglectest the large patrimony and Talent and the thing committed to thy charge
observations.note: The mark of margin note N078, which only names Luke 16, stands after 'Woe be to thee ô Man' and just before these words of the address to man.

observations.quote: who considerest not the Treasure that is hid in thy earthen vessell, and may thereout be digged
observations.note: A treasure is said to be hidden in man's earthen vessel, and it can be dug out of it: the figure of a hidden treasure in man.

observations.name: 2 Cor. 4.
observations.quote: who considerest not the Treasure that is hid in thy earthen vessell
observations.note: The mark of margin note N079, which only names 2 Cor. 4, stands just before these words on the treasure in the earthen vessel.

observations.quote: though he be more in us then we are in our selves, inasmuch as the Spirit of God dwelleth in the midst of our hearts
observations.note: God is said to be more in us than we are in ourselves, because his Spirit dwells in the midst of our hearts.

observations.name: John 14.17.20.
observations.quote: Thou seest not God in thy selfe, whom the world seeth not, neither can receive
observations.note: The mark of margin note N080, which only names John 14.17.20, stands just before these words.

observations.quote: we can learn more in the whole course of our life then that Divine lesson that God hath set us, KNOW THY SELFE.
observations.what: that Divine lesson that God hath set us, KNOW THY SELFE
observations.note: KNOW THY SELFE is set apart in capitals and named the Divine lesson God has set. As the words stand the sentence says 'we can learn more'; the lines given do not show whether a 'not' is meant. The margin note at this place (N081) is a gap of foreign script.

observations.name: Agryppa
observations.quote: it is for a man to know Himselfe; according to the Oracle of Apollo written over the doors of his Temple at Delphos
observations.note: Agryppa, 'holily and learnedly reasoning' about the right way to true Wisdome and Eternall Happinesse, is given the answer: for a man to know himself; the saying is set in accord with the Oracle of Apollo written over the temple doors at Delphos.

observations.name: August.
observations.quote: The first knowledge of God is to know what man is. August.
observations.note: A margin note beside the Agryppa passage gives this saying under the name August.: knowing what man is comes first in knowing God.

observations.quote: man hath the true and Reall possession of all things and Natures in himselfe, as also the speciall and perfect Image even of the Creator of all things
observations.note: Man has in himself all things and natures, and also the image of the Creator.

observations.quote: the knowledge of all things and natures, and of the Creator himselfe (wherein alone true Wisdome and Blessednesse consisteth) must take its rise from the knowledge of a mans selfe
observations.note: Knowledge of all things and of the Creator must begin from a man's knowledge of himself; stated with 'Therefore' as a consequence of the point before. In that knowledge alone wisdom and blessedness consist.

observations.quote: may in himselfe, as in a kind of Deified glasse, behold and understand all things
observations.note: Man who understands himself is likened to a 'Deified glasse' in which all things are seen; 'as in a kind of' marks it as a likeness.

observations.name: David
observations.quote: I am fearfully and wonderfully made, marvellous are thy works.
observations.note: Words given to David, with the place printed in the text as Psal. 139.14, cited in support of man's wonderful make.

observations.quote: He that knoweth himselfe knows God; for God will dwell no where but in man, in whom he is most plaine to be seen. We see God from within.
observations.note: The margin note equates knowing oneself with knowing God, since God dwells only in man and is plainest seen there, and says God is seen from within.

observations.quote: He that knoweth not himselfe cannot have any true intrinsecall and essentiall knowledge of things, but like a bruit beast, what he knows without him, shall remaine without him
observations.note: Without self-knowledge there is no inward, essential knowledge of things; what is known outside stays outside, as with a beast.

observations.quote: there is no knowledge, whether infused from the Heaven, or attained to by labour of industry and earthly diligence, that will abide in the soule for ever
observations.note: Knowledge infused from the Heaven and knowledge won by labour are both said not to last in the soul; one kind is excepted in the words that follow.

observations.quote: but that onely which is inwardly received by Essentiall knowledge in the secret understanding
observations.note: The one knowledge that abides is the one received inwardly, by Essentiall knowledge, in the 'secret understanding'; all other knowledge is subject to forgetfulness.

observations.quote: which Essential intrinsecall knowledge is not from flesh and blood, nor from the multitude of Books and reading, nor from the abundants of Experience and old age
observations.note: The text says what this knowledge does not come from: not flesh and blood, books and reading, experience or age.

observations.name: Dionys. lib. Divinors Nominum.
observations.quote: nor in the inticings of mans Word or wisdome, and warangling of reason
observations.note: The mark of margin note N084, which only names Dionys. and a writing, stands in the list of what essential knowledge does not come from, just before these words.

observations.quote: the mind of man is perfected and compleated by a passive reception of Divine things; not by study and paines; but by patience and submission
observations.note: How the mind is perfected: by passive reception of divine things, patience and submission, not by study.

observations.quote: The whole businesse stands in knowledge, because we are of every thing, and doe carry about every thing in us, even as God himselfe our Father
observations.note: Everything rests on knowledge, because we are of every thing and carry every thing in us, as God does.

observations.name: Joh. 4. & 17.
observations.quote: The Son doth equally posesse all things with his Father
observations.note: The mark of margin note N085, which only names Joh. 4. & 17., stands directly after these words.

observations.quote: as by sin that Divine Character was darkned in us, so sin being satisfied for, & done away, that Character shines out againe more and more
observations.note: All natural and spiritual good things were in man at first; sin darkened this 'Divine Character', and it shines out again when sin is done away.

observations.quote: The Notion of all things is created together with us and in us; and in the very middle of the Spirit by all things hid
observations.note: The notion of all things is created with us and in us, and is said to be hid in the very middle of the Spirit.

observations.quote: we are onely to awake out of our slumbring and snorting, who through sin have fallen asleep in the gifts that God hath bestowed upon us
observations.note: What is asked is only to wake: through sin we have fallen asleep in God's gifts and do not see that they are in us.

observations.quote: The Understanding of man is capable of the highest learning and attainments
observations.note: The author's own statement of what man's understanding can reach, before he gives Plato's wording.

observations.name: Plato
observations.quote: according to Plato, it is full of all Sciences before it be joyned to the body
observations.note: Given to Plato: the understanding is full of all sciences before it is joined to the body. How far the following words on fire in ashes are still Plato's is not shown.

observations.quote: which being oppressed by the body lyeth hid, as fire rak'd up in ashes, but being rouz'd and stirred up from the said humours it shineth forth and discovereth those riches which before lay hid in their Treasures
observations.note: The understanding's knowledge lies hidden under the body like fire raked up in ashes, and once stirred up it shows the riches that lay hid before. The text does not mark where Plato's words end.

observations.quote: stirred up from the said humours
observations.note: 'the said humours' points back to humours named before; the lines given name none before this.

observations.quote: Unlesse all the Treasures of Heavenly and Earthly wisdome were in us before, surely Christ would never have commanded us to seek
observations.note: The author argues from Christ's command to seek: we could find nothing unless God had laid it up in us first.

observations.quote: When we therefore know our selves aright according to both kinds of Light.
observations.note: The text names two kinds of Light by which we know ourselves aright.

observations.quote: (1) according to the Spirit and Nature
observations.what: (1) according to the Spirit and Nature
observations.note: A numbered head directly after 'both kinds of Light', behind the margin note mark. Two readings: (a) a first head whose second the lines given do not show; (b) the words name what the two kinds are, the Spirit and Nature. The lines given show only this '(1)'.

observations.quote: we enter into the gate that is opened in us, and we open to God who stands and knocks at the door of our heart
observations.note: Right self-knowledge is spoken of as entering a gate opened in us and opening the door of the heart to God: a figure, with gate and door placed inside man.

observations.name: Apoc. 3.20.
observations.quote: we open to God who stands and knocks at the door of our heart
observations.note: Margin note N086 ends by naming Apoc. 3.20; its mark stands a few words before this passage on God who stands and knocks.

observations.quote: living according to the will of God, we have all things necessary as well for wisdome as for life, both for present and ever hereafter
observations.note: Living by God's will, we have all that is needed for wisdom and for life, now and hereafter.

observations.quote: From this diligent contemplation & knowledge of a mans self, the true knowledge also of God doth immediately arise (for neither can be absolute & compleat without the other)
observations.note: Knowledge of God arises at once from self-knowledge; neither is complete without the other.

observations.quote: the knowledge of him who IS
observations.note: God is named 'him who IS', with IS in capitals; by considering himself a man may attain a great measure of knowledge of him.

observations.quote: all men being indeed bound to know according to the measure of their capacity
observations.note: All men are bound to know, each as far as he is able.

observations.quote: God is known when the Light of Nature
observations.note: The margin note ties knowing God to the Light of Nature being well understood (one letter of the next word is a gap).

observations.name: Dionysius
observations.quote: Dionysius saith, that we cannot know God from his own Nature, but from that most orderly disposing of all the Creatures proceeding from himselfe
observations.note: Given to Dionysius: God is not known from his own nature but from the ordering of the creatures that come from him.

observations.quote: hold forth as it were images and similitudes of his Divine Presidents or Examples
observations.note: Still within what Dionysius is said to say: the creatures show 'as it were' images of God's 'Presidents or Examples'; the text gives Examples beside Presidents, and '(creatures)' stands in brackets before.

observations.quote: Man that doth not know God, is not known of God; and he that forsakes and rejecteth the knowledge of God, is rejected of God.
observations.note: Who does not know God is not known by him; who rejects that knowledge is rejected. The words follow Dionysius' saying without a mark of where it ends.

observations.quote: He that knoweth not God is inexcusable
observations.note: The margin note at the head of MICRO.6 says that not knowing God cannot be excused.

observations.quote: To be ignorant of God is the Rise or Spring of all diseases, the root of wickedness, by which all vices are increased and grow ripe.
observations.note: Ignorance of God is named the source of all diseases and the root of wickedness.

observations.quote: The more we know God the more we love him, and stedfastly belive in him. He that believes God by loving of him doth cleave to God, he that doth cleave to God is one Spirit with him.
observations.note: The margin note gives a chain: knowing, loving, believing, cleaving, being one Spirit with God.

observations.quote: the perfect righteousnesse, true wisdome, and chiefe happinesse of Man is to know his Principle, God the Creator of all things and to love him in all purity and uprightnesse
observations.note: Man's righteousness, wisdom and happiness are to know and love God, who is here called man's 'Principle'.

observations.name: our Saviour
observations.quote: This is life eternall to know the Father the true God
observations.note: Words given to 'our Saviour', with the place printed in the text as John 17.3., cited for knowledge as eternal life.

observations.quote: viz. That the Believer should acknowledge and worship the Trinity, which knowledge onely giveth eternall life
observations.note: The author adds with 'viz.' what the cited words mean: to acknowledge and worship the Trinity, the only knowledge that gives eternal life.

observations.quote: he that liveth the life of Christ is born the Son of God, he that is born the Son of God must of necessity have the Father, he that hath the Father is sealed with the holy Spirit
observations.note: A chain from living the life of Christ to being born Son of God, having the Father and being sealed with the Spirit.

observations.quote: He that knoweth the Son knoweth the Father also, for they are but one (thing)
observations.note: The word '(thing)' stands in brackets after 'one', an added word marked off from the sentence.

observations.quote: he that knoweth God in Christ is made the habitation and Temple of God, and so is Deified, for he is the Son of God born out of God
observations.note: Knowing God in Christ makes a man God's habitation and temple; the text calls this being 'Deified'.

observations.quote: as by the knowledge of the visible world we come to the knowledge of the invisible Workman
observations.note: From knowing the visible world we come to know its invisible Workman; the text sets beside this that from the visible Christ we learn the Father.

observations.quote: none can rightly know the frame of the world but he that is taught of God
observations.note: Right knowledge of the frame of the world is only for one taught by God.

observations.quote: what the Heathen wrote concerning Nature is for the most part false, because their Phylosophy and other abilities were polluted and corrupt
observations.note: Most of what the Heathen wrote on Nature is called false, their philosophy being corrupt.

observations.quote: In vaine therefore it is to seek knowledge from them who have spent all their life in looking after it
observations.note: It is useless to seek knowledge from the Heathen, who sought it all their lives and found no truth.

observations.quote: many of them were seduced by ignorance rather then malice, the Light of Truth not yet risen to them, nor the Light of Nature as yet kindled by the holy Spirit
observations.note: Many Heathen erred from ignorance, not malice: the Light of Truth had not risen for them and the Light of Nature was not yet kindled by the holy Spirit.

observations.quote: Divinity is the Fountaine of Naturall and Supernaturall knowledge.
observations.note: The margin note makes Divinity the source of both natural and supernatural knowledge.

observations.quote: All true Phylosophy should be grounded on the Scriptures and so return into God
observations.note: True philosophy is to rest on the Scriptures and return into God.

observations.quote: that seed which among the Gentiles was choaked for want of the Sun, like that among the thorns
observations.note: Knowledge among the Gentiles is spoken of as a seed choked for want of the Sun, which regenerate Christians are to reap; the text marks the likeness with 'like'.

observations.quote: No Art can be perfected without Regeneration
observations.note: No art can be brought to perfection without Regeneration.

observations.quote: Christians should not be ruled by Heathen Phylosophy.
observations.note: The margin note states in short the warning against heathen philosophy.

observations.quote: True Phylosophy must be grounded on Christ the corner stone.
observations.note: True philosophy must rest on Christ.

observations.quote: we suffer not the Philosophicall errours of the Heathen to beare down or dominiere over the rules of Christian Phylosophy
observations.note: The text names a 'Christian Phylosophy' with rules of its own and sets it against the errors of the Heathen.

observations.quote: Christians onely in whom the Truth is planted, who have their seed from God, by the means of Regeneration which the Heathen have not
observations.note: Only Christians, through Regeneration, which the Heathen are said to lack, can use or teach philosophy without error.

observations.quote: Believers shall be taught of God when the Holy Spirit is powred forth.
observations.note: Believers will be taught by God when the Holy Spirit is poured out.

observations.quote: the knowledge of God is the Treasury of the whole world wherein all things are laid up, so that without this knowledge no man can come to eternall life
observations.note: Knowledge of God is called the treasury where all things are laid up, and the condition of eternal life.

observations.quote: For Faith, Hope and Love, follow knowledge, Adhaesion or cleaving to followeth Love, Union follows Adhaesion, in Union is Blessednesse and Wisdome.
observations.what: knowledge, Faith, Hope and Love, Adhaesion, Union
observations.note: An ordered series of steps: knowledge; faith, hope and love; adhaesion; union; and in union blessedness and wisdom.

observations.quote: Adhaesion or cleaving to
observations.note: The text gives its own English for Adhaesion: cleaving to.

observations.quote: This Regeneration that holy man Hermes and others of clean hearts and godly lives before the Word was incarnate being enlightned by the holy Spirit, though they concealed it among other Secrets
observations.note: Hermes, a 'holy man', and others of godly life knew Regeneration before the Word was incarnate, being enlightened by the holy Spirit, and concealed it among other Secrets.

observations.quote: they knew it better then many of us who call our selves Christians, and had rather seem to know God then love him
observations.note: These earlier men are said to have known Regeneration better than many Christians, who would rather seem to know God than love him.

observations.quote: This Regeneration that holy man Hermes
observations.note: Here Hermes and others before the Word was incarnate know Regeneration better than many Christians; MICRO.8 says Regeneration is what 'the Heathen have not' and that Christians only use philosophy without error. The lines given do not say whether Hermes is counted among the Heathen.

observations.quote: Man whose mind by Christ is united to God, possesseth the true wisdome of all things, and the most absolute knowledge of all Secrets.
observations.voice: QUOTED: 1 John 4. W{G051: 1 letter illegible}sd. 1. John 17.
observations.note: The man whose mind is united to God through Christ holds the true wisdom of all things and knowledge of all Secrets; announced as 'O great miracle!'.

observations.name: 1 John 4. W{G051: 1 letter illegible}sd. 1. John 17.
observations.quote: O great miracle!
observations.voice: QUOTED: 1 John 4. W{G051: 1 letter illegible}sd. 1. John 17.
observations.note: The mark of margin note N090, which only names writings (1 John 4., a book with a gap, John 17), stands directly after this outcry and before the sentence on the mind united to God.

observations.quote: he that knoweth himselfe, doth know all things Fundamentally in himselfe, and being set between Time and Eternity, above him he sees God eternall, his Creator
observations.note: The self-knower knows all things in himself; he stands between Time and Eternity and sees God above him.

observations.quote: after whose image and likenesse he was with other Angells created by an unsearchable love
observations.note: Man was created after God's image; the words 'with other Angells' set him among the angels.

observations.name: Apoc. 22.
observations.quote: after whose image and likenesse he was with other Angells created
observations.note: Margin note N091 ends by naming Apoc. 22; its mark stands after 'his Creator' and just before these words.

observations.quote: the immortall Angells his fellows and companions, from whom he differeth onely in body and the Judgement to come
observations.note: Beside him are the angels, his fellows; he differs from them only in body and in the Judgement to come.

observations.quote: Under him he sees the visible World whereof he is a pattern, and all the Creatures with whom he hath a likenesse, even his parent of whom he was born as to the externall and mortall body
observations.note: Below him is the visible World, of which man is called a pattern and which is called his 'parent' as to the outer, mortal body.

observations.quote: The soul is the off-spring and image of God.
observations.note: The margin note says it is the soul that is God's offspring and image.

observations.quote: Man who is a true Proteus of a fickle & wavering disposition received a flexible mind from Nature
observations.note: Man is called 'a true Proteus'; the text itself ties the name to a fickle disposition and a flexible mind, able to rise or sink.

observations.name: Eccl. 15.14.
observations.quote: that being set in the midst of the Paradice of this world
observations.note: The mark of margin note N092, which only names Eccl. 15.14, stands after man's flexible mind and just before these words; the same place is named in the text further on in MICRO.10.

observations.quote: by the assistance of Divine Grace raising himselfe upward he might be regenerated into a quiet Angell or, the Forger of his fortune winding and creeping downward degenerate into a restlesse Bruite
observations.note: Two ways are open to man: upward by grace, regenerated into an angel, or downward by his own doing, degenerating into a brute.

observations.name: Gen 2.
observations.quote: neglecting the fatherly admonition, and his due obedience
observations.note: The mark of margin note N093, which only names Gen 2, stands directly after these words on man neglecting the fatherly admonition.

observations.quote: turning from the mean to (the extreame) himselfe, dispising his Creator
observations.note: The fall is told as a turning from 'the mean' to himself as an extreme; '(the extreame)' stands in brackets as an added word.

observations.quote: learned by experience what his own proper Evill and Nothing was to his voluntary damage and perdition, like a Thief and Robber
observations.note: By turning to himself man learned his own 'Evill and Nothing', to his own willing loss; he is likened to a thief and robber.

observations.quote: theft and robbery of himselfe, and death
observations.note: The margin note speaks of one who 'seeks to himself that which is anothers' and names with 'i. e.' the two things he falls into: theft and robbery of himself, and death; much of the note is gaps.

observations.quote: he made choise of death rather then of life, and like Lucifer, not content with his lot, ambitiously desiring higher things, he set himselfe in opposition against God
observations.note: Man chose death, and like Lucifer desired higher things and set himself against God.

observations.quote: cast out of the Garden of pleasures into this dolefull and darksome valley of Misery and Ignorance
observations.note: The fall ends in being cast out of the 'Garden of pleasures' into a valley of Misery and Ignorance.

observations.name: Eccl. 15.14.
observations.quote: The first man was left in the hand of his own counsell (Eccl. 15.14.)
observations.note: The text itself names Eccl. 15.14 for the saying that the first man was left to his own counsel.

observations.name: Herms and Moses
observations.quote: greedily desired the possession of good and evill to his own destruction, as Herms and Moses
observations.note: Herms and Moses are named together as showing that the first man desired good and evil to his own destruction (the next word has a gap); the book spells 'Herms' here and 'Hermes' in MICRO.9.

observations.quote: Man, the bond or buckle of the world, the last wonderfull and honourable living creature
observations.what: the bond or buckle of the world
observations.note: Man is named the bond or buckle of the world and the last living creature.

observations.quote: God created man that the number and losse of the rebellious Angells might be made up
observations.note: The margin note at the head of MICRO.11 gives the purpose of man's creation: to make up the number of the rebellious angels (the last word of the note has a gap).

observations.quote: was, upon the sixt day, after all other things, drawn or taken
observations.note: The making of man is told as a step of work: on the sixth day, after everything else, he was drawn or taken out of something (the text adds 'è limo terrae' in brackets).

observations.quote: out of the slime of the Earth or visible frame of the whole consisting of Heaven or Heavenly Sphaeres and the Earth
observations.note: The 'slime of the Earth' (è limo terrae) is glossed as the visible frame of the whole, Heaven and the Earth together, not earth alone.

observations.quote: viz. out of the most thin or pure substance of the whole frame of the world concentred into one body
observations.note: With 'viz.' the text narrows what man was made of: the thinnest or purest substance of the whole frame of the world, brought together into one body.

observations.quote: fashioned by the great Spacyrus into a bodily shape, made to supply the place of the fallen Angells
observations.note: The pure substance is fashioned into a bodily shape by one named 'the great Spacyrus'; man is made to fill the place of the fallen angels.

observations.quote: Man was formed of the most excellent Compound and purest Extract of the whole Word, out of the Center of all Circles
observations.note: Man is formed of a 'Compound' and 'Extract' of the whole; the text prints 'Word' here, where the lines around it speak of the world.

observations.name: Nazianzen
observations.quote: God made Man last, that in him, as in a short and briefe way, he might set out or expresse all that before he had made at large
observations.note: Given to Nazianzen, speaking of the workmanship of man: man was made last so that all the parts of the world might be expressed in him in brief.

observations.quote: As an Oration is made up of letters and sillables, so the Microcosm or Limus Terrae, Man is compacted of all bodies and created things.
observations.note: A likeness: as a speech is built of letters and syllables, man is put together out of all bodies and created things.

observations.quote: the Microcosm or Limus Terrae, Man is compacted of all bodies and created things
observations.note: Three names are again set together for one thing: Microcosm, Limus Terrae, Man.

observations.quote: took the Quintessence out of all things created and thereof fashioned and composed Man as the Prince and End of all these
observations.note: God's making of man told as work: the Quintessence is taken out of all created things and man is fashioned from it.

observations.quote: congratulated him as his Son holding or possessing the honourable place of the high Divinity on Earth
observations.note: God greets man as his Son, who holds the place of the Divinity on earth.

observations.quote: In respect of the Body or corruptible Nature he bears the Image of the great, sensible and temporall World
observations.note: As to the body, man bears the image of the great, sensible world.

observations.quote: he bears the Image of the great, sensible and temporall World
observations.note: Here man bears the image of the world; MICRO.10 says the visible world is that 'whereof he is a pattern', and MICRO.12 calls the Archetype the 'originall copy and patterne of the world'. Which of the two is the pattern of the other rests on the word 'pattern'.

observations.quote: the Archetype or originall copy and patterne of the world, that is, of the immortall Wisdome of God himselfe
observations.note: As to the soul, man bears the image of the Archetype, which the text explains as the original copy and pattern of the world, that is, God's immortal Wisdom.

observations.quote: all the properties of Animalls, Vegetables and Mineralls entred into him
observations.note: All the properties of animals, vegetables and minerals entered into man.

observations.quote: God is all things of himselfe; Man is made all things of God, and was therefore created last that by him the compleatnesse and perfection of all the Creatures might be signified.
observations.note: God is all things of himself, man is made all things by God; created last, man signifies the completeness of all creatures.

observations.quote: Man is the tye, bond, knot, joynt
observations.what: the tye, bond, knot, joynt, packet or bundle of all the Creatures
observations.note: A run of names for man as what holds all creatures together; after the note mark it goes on 'packet or bundle of all the Creatures'.

observations.name: Psal. 8.
observations.quote: Thou hast put all things under his
observations.note: The margin note beside the names for man gives words under the name Psal. 8 (the last word has a gap).

observations.name: Parace{G068: 1 letter illegible}s.
observations.quote: excepteth the Spirits and inhabitant of the
observations.note: The same margin note reports that a named writer (the name has a gap) makes an exception for the Spirits and inhabitant of certain Elements (gap before 'Elements') to all things being put under man.

observations.quote: they respect and honour him as Gods steward set over the Orchard or Garden of this world
observations.note: All created things honour man as God's steward over the garden of this world.

observations.quote: God is the Center and Circle of all things that he brought out of himselfe
observations.what: the Center and Circle of all things
observations.note: God is named both Center and Circle of all that he brought out of himself.

observations.quote: all the works of the Divine goodnesse are circular and perfect, sphaerically wheeled about to him from whom they proceeded
observations.note: God's works are circular: they wheel back to him from whom they came.

observations.quote: He is the Centre in that all things flow from him, and because the Essence of all things pierceth also through all things
observations.note: The text says in what sense God is Centre: all things flow from him and the essence of all things pierces through all things.

observations.quote: God the Centre and Circle of all things.
observations.what: God the Centre and Circle of all things
observations.note: The margin note heads the passage with the same two names.

observations.quote: He is the Circle, because like an all-capacious Tabernacle he concludeth and comprehendeth all things.
observations.note: The text says in what sense God is Circle: he encloses and holds all things, like a tabernacle.

observations.quote: Within God are all things, and at the worlds end nothing shall be without him
observations.note: All things are within God, and at the world's end nothing will be outside him.

observations.quote: So is Man.
observations.note: This margin note carries on from the note before it (N097, God the Centre and Circle of all things) and applies the same to man.

observations.quote: Thus Man in imitation of his Creator is the Centre of the Creatures, and the Circle of them all.
observations.note: Man, imitating his Creator, is both Centre and Circle of the creatures.

observations.quote: It was Gods pleasure that all things which he made should honour him by Man.
observations.note: The margin note says all made things were to honour God through man.

observations.quote: all things in the world doe not onely look to him as their Guide and Governour, for whom also they were all created
observations.note: All things look to man as guide and governor and were created for him.

observations.quote: on him all the Sphaeres bestow their beams, operations, reflections and influences, and on him all the Creatures poure their vertues and effects
observations.note: The spheres send their beams and influences upon man, and the creatures pour their virtues and effects on him.

observations.quote: as upon a middle Point and Retinacle or that by which they are stayed and supported
observations.note: The creatures pour their virtues on man as on a middle point; 'Retinacle' is explained as that by which they are stayed and supported.

observations.quote: As the Earth is a Receptive body of all seeds, so also is Man.
observations.note: The margin note likens man to the earth, a body that receives all seeds.

observations.quote: Man is said to be the Circle in that he containeth all things in himselfe
observations.note: The text says in what sense man is the Circle: he contains all things and leads them back with himself to the source they flowed from.

observations.quote: that Summum Bonum, or chiefest good
observations.note: The text gives its own English for Summum Bonum: chiefest good; man leads all things back to it as the fountain of Eternity.

dropped.reason: Hermes is named and called holy, but no words are given to him; what the text says of him is kept in the concealment observation from A63, B76, B77.
